title: Southern Rhône
description: Sun, stones and the Mistral: Grenache-led blends from Châteauneuf-du-Pape to Côtes du Rhône.
L: South of Montélimar, the Rhône valley opens into a wide plain dotted with hills, around Avignon and Orange. The southern Rhône makes over 90% of all Rhône wine. Soils vary: large round stones, galets roulés, sand, clay and limestone. Côtes du Rhône covers the whole region.

The climate is Mediterranean: hot, dry summers, mild winters and plenty of sun. The Mistral, a cold, dry wind from the north, blows often, sometimes over 90 km/h. It dries vines after rain, reducing disease, and cools them, but can break shoots. Organic farming is common because conditions are healthy.
How does the Mistral help vineyards?
It dries vines after rain, reducing disease
A dry wind keeps grapes healthy.

In the 14th century, the popes moved to Avignon. They built a summer castle, the Châteauneuf-du-Pape, the pope's new castle, and planted vines. In 1923, Baron Le Roy of Châteauneuf drew up rules for the area's wine, which helped inspire France's AOC system, created in 1935.
Châteauneuf-du-Pape's rules in the 1920s helped inspire the French AOC system.
Yes. Baron Le Roy's 1923 rules were a model.
The southern Rhône makes over 90% of Rhône wine
Its Mediterranean climate and the Mistral keep vines healthy
The popes at Avignon gave Châteauneuf its name
Name the southern Rhône's main grapes

Grenache is the main red grape, loving heat and drought, giving red fruit, spice and high alcohol. Syrah adds colour and structure; Mourvèdre adds tannin and savoury, gamey notes; Cinsault adds perfume and lightness, especially in rosé. Carignan also appears. Blends of Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre are called GSM.

White grapes include Grenache Blanc, Clairette, Roussanne, Marsanne, Bourboulenc and Viognier. White wines are a small share, about 7%, but growing. They're rich, with stone fruit, herbs and moderate acidity. Châteauneuf-du-Pape Blanc is the most famous.
Match each grape to its role.
Côtes du Rhône red must be mainly Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre. It's one of France's best everyday reds.
GSM is Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre.
Grenache leads, with Syrah, Mourvèdre and Cinsault
GSM blends balance fruit, colour and structure
Whites are a small, growing share

Châteauneuf-du-Pape's most famous soil is covered with galets roulés, large, round quartzite stones left by the ancient Rhône. They store heat by day and release it at night, helping ripening, and protect the soil from drying. But Châteauneuf also has sand, which gives elegant wines like Château Rayas, and limestone.

Châteauneuf allows 13 grape varieties, counted as 18 including colour variants: red, white and pink. Grenache usually dominates, often 70% or more. Château de Beaucastel famously uses all 13. Yields are low, about 35 hl/ha. Wines are rich, warm, spicy, with red fruit, garrigue herbs and leather, often 14.5 to 15.5% alcohol.
Large round stones that store heat
These river stones warm the vines at night.

Many Châteauneuf bottles carry the papal coat of arms embossed on the glass. Most of the wine is red; about 7% is white. Good Châteauneuf ages 10 to 20 years, gaining leather, game and dried fruit. Neighbouring Gigondas and Vacqueyras offer similar, often more affordable wines.
Galets roulés store heat in Châteauneuf's vineyards
Its rich, spicy reds age 10 to 20 years

Tavel, across the river from Châteauneuf, is France's only appellation for rosé alone. Its rosé is darker and fuller than Provence's, made from Grenache, Cinsault and others with longer skin contact. It's a rosé for food, able to age a few years. Lirac, nearby, makes red, white and rosé.

Beaumes-de-Venise makes Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise, a vin doux naturel: fermentation is stopped by adding grape spirit, keeping natural sugar, at 15% or more alcohol. It's golden, with orange blossom, peach and grape. Rasteau also makes a fortified Grenache vin doux naturel, red or amber.
What is a vin doux naturel?
A wine fortified during fermentation to keep sugar
Spirit stops the yeast, leaving natural sweetness.

Besides Châteauneuf and Tavel, the southern Rhône crus include Gigondas, Vacqueyras, Rasteau, Cairanne, Vinsobres, Lirac and Beaumes-de-Venise. Below them sit Côtes du Rhône Villages, sometimes with a village name, and then Côtes du Rhône. Each step up means stricter rules and usually more character.
Hermitage is in the northern Rhône.
Crus sit above Villages and Côtes du Rhône
Reading the Rhône and eating with it

Labels run from Côtes du Rhône, the base, to Côtes du Rhône Villages, to Villages with a named village, like Séguret or Plan de Dieu, to the crus like Gigondas and Châteauneuf-du-Pape. Grapes are rarely named. Prices rise with each step, but good Villages wines are excellent value.

Southern Rhône reds suit Provençal food: lamb with herbs, daube, a beef stew, ratatouille, grilled sausages and game. Tavel suits grilled fish, bouillabaisse and charcuterie. Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise suits fruit tarts, melon and blue cheese. Serve reds at 16 to 17 degrees; high alcohol feels hot if served too warm.
Order these labels from broadest to most specific.
Each step tightens the rules and the area.
Good Côtes du Rhône Villages from a top producer often tastes like a junior Châteauneuf-du-Pape at a fraction of the price.
Herbs and lamb echo its garrigue and spice.
Labels run from Côtes du Rhône to the crus
Reds suit lamb, daube and ratatouille
Serve not too warm; good Villages offer value
Describe the southern Rhône's climate and grapes
Match each wine to its style.
The southern Rhône makes many styles.
A cold, dry wind from the north.
The southern Rhône makes most of the Rhône's wine.
Which grapes are common in southern Rhône reds?
Pinot Noir isn't a Rhône grape.
The southern Rhône is sunny, windy and Grenache-led
Tavel and Beaumes-de-Venise add rosé and sweet styles
Côtes du Rhône Villages offer great value
